standard_prerequisites.name: Nash-Williams arboricity theorem
standard_prerequisites.statement: A finite multigraph decomposes into k edge-disjoint forests if and only if every nonempty edge subset F' satisfies |F'| <= k(|V(F')| - 1); cited by the author at source line 214.

standard_prerequisites.name: Butterfly bookkeeping
standard_prerequisites.statement: The (k1,k2)-fold butterfly graph of a bipartite graph carries k1k2 copies of every edge, so an edge count for the bipartite graph is recovered by summing over the k1k2 pairs of vertex classes.

core_obligations: Direction sparsity implies arboricity: after adding any l-1 edges between the two sides, apply the Nash-Williams sparsity criterion to the resulting butterfly multigraph and bound |F(V')| by summing |F(V'_{1,i} union V'_{2,j})| over the k1k2 pairs of copies, obtaining |F(V')| <= k1k2(|V'| - 1) (source lines 203-213).

Direction arboricity implies sparsity: starting from the forest decomposition of the butterfly graph, add the l-1 edges inside V'_1 union V'_2 and read the resulting inequality back as the (k1,k2,l)-sparsity inequality of the original bipartite graph, keeping track of the k1k2 factor introduced by the added edges (source lines 201-202).
Keep the two added-edge counts exact in both directions, since the equivalence is asserted for every choice of the l-1 added edges and not merely for one of them.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is the bipartite sparsity/arboricity equivalence of source lines 196-199, in which the auxiliary object is the (k1,k2)-fold butterfly multigraph of the bipartite graph and the hypothesis is that one may add any l-1 edges between the two sides. The work is entirely in the two counting chains at 201-202 and 208-213: the first has to convert a forest-decomposition bound of the butterfly graph into the sparsity inequality of the bipartite graph while carrying the (l-1)k1k2 added edges, and the second has to sum the per-copy sparsity bounds over all k1k2 vertex-class pairs to reach the Nash-Williams form. Neither direction is a direct restatement of the cited Nash-Williams theorem, and the butterfly construction itself is defined at 194.

editorial_notes: In the source the theorem's own label is written after the statement text (source line 198); the retained span covers the whole theorem environment, label included.

The two citations inside the retained lines (Servatius on k-plane matroids; Nash-Williams on edge-disjoint spanning trees) are resolved by a flattened two-entry bibliography fragment, so no bibliography database and no BibTeX run is needed.

The theorem is stated in the source with k1, k2, l in the positive integers and k1 + k2 > l, although the surrounding discussion also treats l in the nonnegative integers; the statement is retained verbatim and no hypothesis was added.
The retained environments print with this package's own numbering rather than the numbering of the article's full document.

editorial_scope: One original exact result: the equivalence between (k1,k2,l)-sparsity of a bipartite graph and the forest decomposition of its butterfly multigraph after adding any l-1 edges.
